claim: CLC channels mediate passive Cl− conduction.
source: CLC channels mediate passive Cl− conduction, while CLC transporters mediate active Cl− transport coupled to H+ transport in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CLC channels supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: CLC transporters mediate active Cl− transport coupled to H+ transport in the opposite direction.
source: CLC channels mediate passive Cl− conduction, while CLC transporters mediate active Cl− transport coupled to H+ transport in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CLC transporters supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The distinction between CLC-0/1/2 channels and CLC transporters seems undetectable by amino acid sequence.
source: The distinction between CLC-0/1/2 channels and CLC transporters seems undetectable by amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the structural study and is supported by the difficulty in distinguishing these proteins by sequence analysis.

claim: The human CLC-1 channel structure was determined.
source: To understand why they are different functionally we determined the structure of the human CLC-1 channel.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cryo-EM structure determination of CLC-1.

claim: The 'glutamate gate' residue in CLC-1 adopts a location in the structure that appears to preclude it from its transport function.
source: Its 'glutamate gate' residue, known to mediate proton transfer in CLC transporters, adopts a location in the structure that appears to preclude it from its transport function.
evidence: This is based on structural observations from the cryo-EM structure showing the glutamate gate in a different position than in transporters.

claim: Smaller side chains in CLC-1 produce a wider pore near the intracellular surface, potentially reducing a kinetic barrier for Cl− conduction.
source: Furthermore, smaller side chains produce a wider pore near the intracellular surface, potentially reducing a kinetic barrier for Cl− conduction.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing pore dimensions between CLC-1 and transporters.

claim: When the corresponding residues are mutated in a transporter, it is converted to a channel.
source: When the corresponding residues are mutated in a transporter, it is converted to a channel.
evidence: This is supported by functional experiments on EcCLC mutants described in the manuscript.

claim: Cl− at key sites in the pore appear to interact with reduced affinity compared to transporters.
source: Finally, Cl− at key sites in the pore appear to interact with reduced affinity compared to transporters.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of density at Scen in the CLC-1 structure.

claim: Subtle differences in glutamate gate conformation, internal pore diameter and Cl− affinity distinguish CLC channels and transporters.
source: Thus, subtle differences in glutamate gate conformation, internal pore diameter and Cl− affinity distinguish CLC channels and transporters.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data presented.

claim: Channel-forming CLCs are passive Cl− conductors.
source: Channel-forming CLCs are passive Cl− conductors (Jentsch et al., 1990; Miller and White, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Transporter-forming CLCs exchange, with fixed stoichiometry, two Cl− ions and one proton (H+) in opposite directions.
source: transporter-forming CLCs exchange, with fixed stoichiometry, two Cl− ions and one proton (H+) in opposite directions (i.e., they are Cl−/H+ antiporters) (Accardi and Miller, 2004; Picollo and Pusch, 2005; Scheel et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: At the level of amino acid sequence, the distinction between CLC channels and transporters is not apparent.
source: The puzzling aspect of this dual functionality within the CLC protein family is that at the level of amino acid sequence, the distinction between the channels and transporters is not apparent.
evidence: This is stated as a known observation that motivates the study.

claim: Channels are described as pores with one gate.
source: channels are described as pores with one gate and transporters as pores with two gates that are never permitted to open simultaneously (Figure 1) (for review see [Gadsby, 2009])
evidence: This is a conceptual model supported by a review citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Transporters are described as pores with two gates that are never permitted to open simultaneously.
source: channels are described as pores with one gate and transporters as pores with two gates that are never permitted to open simultaneously (Figure 1) (for review see [Gadsby, 2009])
evidence: This is a conceptual model supported by a review citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: CLC channels seem to fall under the category of channels that emerged from a family of transporters.
source: CLC channels seem to fall under this category of channels that emerged from a family of transporters (Accardi and Picollo, 2010; Lísal and Maduke, 2008; Miller, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: CLC transporter structures show a narrow Cl− transport pathway with three consecutive Cl−-binding sites, referred to as Sext, Scen and Sint.
source: CLC transporter structures show a narrow Cl− transport pathway with three consecutive Cl−-binding sites, referred to as Sext, Scen and Sint, for external (nearest the extracellular solution), central and internal (nearest the intracellular solution), respectively.
evidence: This is based on previous structural studies of CLC transporters.

claim: Chloride is observed at Sext, Scen, and Sint sites in various CLC transporter structures.
source: Chloride is observed at these sites in various structures (Dutzler et al., 2002; Dutzler et al., 2003; Feng et al., 2010; Jayaram et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by cited structural studies.

claim: CLC transporters all contain a glutamate residue positioned such that its side chain carboxylate group can bind either at Sext or Scen – in competition with a Cl− ion – or reside in the extracellular solution.
source: In addition, the transporters all contain a glutamate residue positioned such that its side chain carboxylate group can bind either at Sext or Scen – in competition with a Cl− ion – or reside in the extracellular solution.
evidence: This is based on structural observations from previous studies.

claim: The glutamate side chain might transfer a proton from inside to out (or the reverse) when it moves between its Scen position to its extracellular position.
source: This led to the idea that glutamate might not only be a competitor for the Cl− binding sites as the structures suggest, but it might also transfer a proton from inside to out (or the reverse) when it moves between its Scen position to its extracellular position (Feng et al., 2010; Feng et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by cited references.

claim: The proton transfer mechanism would naturally give rise to the 2:1 Cl−:H+ exchange stoichiometry characteristic of CLC transporters because 2 Cl− ions must be displaced when the glutamate gate moves between the extracellular solution and Scen.
source: The transfer would naturally give rise to the 2:1 Cl−:H+ exchange stoichiometry characteristic of CLC transporters because 2 Cl− ions must be displaced when the glutamate gate moves between the extracellular solution and Scen.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on structural and functional data.

claim: Mutation of the glutamate gate in a CLC transporter converts it into a passive (but slow) Cl− channel.
source: This mechanism is consistent with the demonstrated conversion of a CLC transporter into a passive (but slow) Cl− channel upon mutation of the glutamate, as well as the demonstrated ability of small carboxylate-containing organic acids to compete with Cl− inside the pore (Accardi et al., 2004; Accardi and Miller, 2004; Feng et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: Small carboxylate-containing organic acids can compete with Cl− inside the pore of CLC transporters.
source: This mechanism is consistent with the demonstrated conversion of a CLC transporter into a passive (but slow) Cl− channel upon mutation of the glutamate, as well as the demonstrated ability of small carboxylate-containing organic acids to compete with Cl− inside the pore (Accardi et al., 2004; Accardi and Miller, 2004; Feng et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: There must exist a relatively high kinetic barrier to Cl− flow near the intracellular side of the pore in CLC transporters.
source: But there was one important caveat to make this transporter mechanism work: there must exist a relatively high kinetic barrier to Cl− flow near the intracellular side of the pore (Feng et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a mechanistic requirement supported by a cited reference.

claim: The kinetic barrier near the intracellular side would serve as the 'second gate' in the gating model conceptualization of transporters.
source: This barrier would serve as the 'second gate' in the gating model conceptualization of transporters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and functional data in the context of the gating model.

claim: CLC transporters have a channel-like pore.
source: So far, data for CLC transporters seem consistent with this mechanism: they have a channel-like pore, an external 'glutamate gate' that competes with Cl− binding and (presumably) transfers H+ across the membrane, and structurally what appears to be a relatively high resistance (i.e., a large kinetic barrier) to Cl− flow near the intracellular aspect of the pore (i.e., the pore there is very narrow.)
evidence: This is based on structural observations.

claim: CLC transporters have an external 'glutamate gate' that competes with Cl− binding and (presumably) transfers H+ across the membrane.
source: So far, data for CLC transporters seem consistent with this mechanism: they have a channel-like pore, an external 'glutamate gate' that competes with Cl− binding and (presumably) transfers H+ across the membrane, and structurally what appears to be a relatively high resistance (i.e., a large kinetic barrier) to Cl− flow near the intracellular aspect of the pore (i.e., the pore there is very narrow.)
evidence: This is based on structural and functional data from previous studies.

claim: CLC transporters have structurally what appears to be a relatively high resistance (i.e., a large kinetic barrier) to Cl− flow near the intracellular aspect of the pore.
source: So far, data for CLC transporters seem consistent with this mechanism: they have a channel-like pore, an external 'glutamate gate' that competes with Cl− binding and (presumably) transfers H+ across the membrane, and structurally what appears to be a relatively high resistance (i.e., a large kinetic barrier) to Cl− flow near the intracellular aspect of the pore (i.e., the pore there is very narrow.)
evidence: This is based on structural observations showing a narrow pore.

claim: Only one CLC channel structure has been determined, CLC-K from Bos taurus.
source: Only one CLC channel structure has been determined, CLC-K from Bos taurus (referred to as bCLC-K or shortly CLC-K) (Park et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the state of structural knowledge at the time, supported by a citation.

claim: CLC-K can be distinguished from CLC transporters based on its amino acid sequence because it does not have a 'glutamate gate'.
source: This is a special case, a rare type of CLC channel that can be distinguished from CLC transporters based on its amino acid sequence because it does not have a 'glutamate gate'.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural knowledge.

claim: The absence of a 'glutamate gate' renders CLC-K inert to H+ transfer.
source: That difference alone renders CLC-K inert to H+ transfer.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the mechanism of H+ transfer in transporters.

claim: The structure of CLC-K revealed a wider pore diameter on the intracellular side, consistent with a lowered kinetic barrier to Cl− flow.
source: The structure of CLC-K also revealed a wider pore diameter on the intracellular side, consistent with a lowered kinetic barrier to Cl− flow.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of CLC-K.

claim: CLC-0/1/2 channels contain a 'glutamate gate' and are not distinguishable from CLC transporters by sequence.
source: CLC-0/1/2 channels, by contrast, contain a 'glutamate gate' and are not distinguishable from CLC transporters by sequence.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: CLC-1 plays an important role in membrane repolarization of skeletal muscle cells following muscular contraction.
source: We are also interested in the CLC-1 channel because it plays an important role in membrane repolarization of skeletal muscle cells following muscular contraction, and its mutation in humans causes hereditary muscle disorders known as myotonia congenita (George et al., 1993; Koch et al., 1992; Lorenz et al., 1994; Steinmeyer et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Mutation of CLC-1 in humans causes hereditary muscle disorders known as myotonia congenita.
source: We are also interested in the CLC-1 channel because it plays an important role in membrane repolarization of skeletal muscle cells following muscular contraction, and its mutation in humans causes hereditary muscle disorders known as myotonia congenita (George et al., 1993; Koch et al., 1992; Lorenz et al., 1994; Steinmeyer et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: CLC-1 protein was purified in mild detergent from cultured human cells.
source: We purified the CLC-1 protein in mild detergent from cultured human cells and examined them by cryo-EM single particle analysis (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used.

claim: CLC-1 particles showed good contrast on micrographs under the optimized freezing and data acquisition conditions.
source: Despite its small molecular size (200 kDa), particles showed good contrast on micrographs under the optimized freezing and data acquisition conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two-dimensional (2D) class averages of selected CLC-1 particles displayed 2-fold rotational symmetry around an axis normal to the membrane.
source: Two-dimensional (2D) class averages of selected particles displayed 2-fold rotational symmetry around an axis normal to the membrane (detergent micelle) (Figure 2B), as expected from the homodimeric architecture of CLC proteins (Dutzler et al., 2002; Ludewig et al., 1996; Miller and White, 1984)
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2B, consistent with known CLC architecture.

claim: A density map of CLC-1 was reconstructed at 3.9 Å resolution with C2 symmetry imposed.
source: After removing artifacts and damaged particles by 2D classification, a density map was reconstructed at 3.9 Å resolution with C2 symmetry imposed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the result of the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The CLC-1 density map showed a well-resolved transmembrane domain (TMD) with clearly visible α-helical features.
source: This map showed a well-resolved transmembrane domain (TMD) with clearly visible α-helical features.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: Density for the carboxy-terminal cytosolic domain (CTD) of CLC-1 was lower quality, suggesting conformational flexibility in this region.
source: By contrast, density for the carboxy-terminal cytosolic domain (CTD) was lower quality, suggesting conformational flexibility in this region.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map and an inference about flexibility.

claim: The resolution of the TMD of CLC-1 was improved to 3.4 Å using masking techniques.
source: Using masking techniques to isolate individual regions, the resolution of the TMD was further improved to 3.4 Å (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Video 1).
evidence: This describes the result of focused refinement.

claim: The CTD of CLC-1 remained poorly defined, likely due to continuous pivotal movements of its two wing-like structures.
source: The CTD remained poorly defined, likely due to continuous pivotal movements of its two wing-like structures (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation and inference from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The good quality TMD density map enabled building a molecular model that included nearly all side chains.
source: The good quality TMD density map enabled building a molecular model that included nearly all side chains (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Video 1).
evidence: This describes the model building process.

claim: The crystal structure of the CLC-0 CTD was docked into the CLC-1 CTD map with confidence.
source: The CTD map did not show side chain density but we could dock with confidence the crystal structure of the CLC-0 CTD (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Meyer and Dutzler, 2006).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for the CTD.

claim: Both CLC-1 and CLC-0 channels contain a large loop extending from the CTD's cystathionin-β-synthase (CBS) domains, which was not visible in either the EM density map or the crystal structure.
source: Both CLC-1 and CLC-0 channels contain a large loop extending from the CTD's cystathionin-β-synthase (CBS) domains, which was not visible in either the EM density map or the crystal structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The function of the CTD is poorly understood.
source: The function of the CTD is poorly understood; it may even be dispensable for ion transport given its high tolerance to mutation (Estévez et al., 2004) and absence in most bacterial CLC transporters.
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies and structural observations.

claim: The CTD may be dispensable for ion transport given its high tolerance to mutation and absence in most bacterial CLC transporters.
source: The function of the CTD is poorly understood; it may even be dispensable for ion transport given its high tolerance to mutation (Estévez et al., 2004) and absence in most bacterial CLC transporters.
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies and structural observations.

claim: The TMD of CLC-1 exhibits the canonical dimeric architecture of a CLC protein.
source: The TMD of CLC-1 exhibits the canonical dimeric architecture of a CLC protein (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: Each monomer of CLC-1 contains a complete ion transport pathway that appears structurally independent from that of the neighboring monomer.
source: Each monomer is roughly a triangular prism shape and contains a complete ion transport pathway that appears structurally independent from that of the neighboring monomer.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: The Cl− transport pore in CLC-1 is most narrowly constricted halfway across the membrane, within the region referred to as the selectivity filter.
source: As in other CLC structures (Dutzler et al., 2002; Dutzler et al., 2003; Feng et al., 2010; Park et al., 2017), the Cl− transport pore in CLC-1 is most narrowly constricted halfway across the membrane, within the region referred to as the selectivity filter (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure, consistent with other CLC structures.

claim: The pore lining of CLC-1 is charged positive to attract Cl−.
source: Overall, the pore lining is charged positive to attract Cl− (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on electrostatic calculations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The potential route for ion diffusion in CLC-1 is bifurcated on the intracellular side of the selectivity filter.
source: In contrast to other CLC proteins the potential route for ion diffusion in CLC-1 is bifurcated on the intracellular side of the selectivity filter– one following the canonical Cl− transport pathway found in all CLC proteins and the 'second' pore directed toward the protomer-protomer boundary on the cytosolic surface, which is distinctive in CLC-1 (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: Both branches of the bifurcation in CLC-1 are potentially hydrated because the radius is greater than that of water (1.4 Å) and the linings contain chemical groups with hydrogen bonding potential.
source: Both branches of the bifurcation are potentially hydrated because the radius is greater than that of water (1.4 Å) and the linings contain chemical groups with hydrogen bonding potential.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of pore dimensions and chemical properties.

claim: A branch equivalent to CLC-1's secondary pore in the CLC-K channel is sealed off by F222 and V226 due to a different αH helix position.
source: A branch equivalent to CLC-1's secondary pore in the CLC-K channel is sealed off by F222 and V226 (corresponding to F288 and V292 of CLC-1) due to a different αH helix position (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between CLC-1 and CLC-K.

claim: In transporters, only a much narrower (~0.9–1.0 Å radius) pore could be detected at the position equivalent to CLC-1's secondary pore, where stable dwelling of water molecules seems unlikely.
source: In transporters, only a much narrower (~0.9–1.0 Å radius) pore could be detected, where stable dwelling of water molecules seems unlikely (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of transporters.

claim: In the E. coli transporter (EcCLC), the pore equivalent to CLC-1's secondary pore is further capped near the cytosolic surface by E203.
source: In the E. coli transporter (EcCLC), the pore is further capped near the cytosolic surface by E203 (corresponding to V292 of CLC-1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of EcCLC.

claim: E203 of EcCLC and the equivalent Glu of mammalian CLC-4 and CLC-5 transporters have been implicated in shuttling H+ between the intracellular solvent and the protein interior by side-chain protonation and deprotonation.
source: We note that E203 of EcCLC and the equivalent Glu of mammalian CLC-4 and CLC-5 transporters have been implicated in shuttling H+ between the intracellular solvent and the protein interior (Lim and Miller, 2009; Lim et al., 2012; Zdebik et al., 2008) by side-chain protonation and deprotonation
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: The E203 feature does not seem to be essential for H+ transport in other cases, including the C. merolae transporter (CmCLC).
source: although this feature does not seem to be essential for H+ transport in other cases, including the C. merolae transporter (CmCLC) (Feng et al., 2010; Feng et al., 2012; Phillips et al., 2012)
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: During Cl−/H+ exchange cycles, the αH helix of transporters may transiently undergo a conformational change such that a water-accessible pore is formed similarly to the CLC-1 case, which might facilitate H+ transfer.
source: It is possible that during Cl−/H+ exchange cycles, the αH helix of transporters transiently undergoes a conformational change such that a water-accessible pore is formed similarly to the CLC-1 case, which might facilitate H+ transfer.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: The CLC-1 channel does not transport H+ in a manner tightly coupled to Cl−.
source: Unlike transporter-type CLCs, the CLC-1 channel does not transport H+ in a manner tightly coupled to Cl−
evidence: This is based on functional characterization of CLC-1.

claim: It is unclear whether CLC-1's second intracellular pore is utilized for ion transport.
source: and thus it is unclear whether CLC-1's second intracellular pore is utilized for ion transport.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the functional role of the second pore.

claim: Cl− ions may move through CLC-1's second intracellular pore in addition to the primary Cl− pathway.
source: Cl− ions may move through this pore in addition to the primary Cl− pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The CLC-1 structure shows an anion selectivity filter largely similar to other CLC proteins but with some distinctive features.
source: The CLC-1 structure shows an anion selectivity filter largely similar to other CLC proteins but with some distinctive features (Figure 4A and Video 2).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The filter in CLC-1 is formed at the central constriction of the Cl− pathway by αN, αF, and αD helices, all of which point their N-terminal ends towards the center where Cl−-binding sites are formed.
source: The filter is formed at the central constriction of the Cl− pathway by αN, αF, and αD helices, all of which point their N-terminal ends towards the center where Cl−-binding sites are formed.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: The arrangement of αN, αF, and αD helices contributes to an electrostatically positive environment at the Cl−-binding sites through α-helix end charges.
source: This arrangement contributes to an electrostatically positive environment at the Cl−-binding sites through α-helix end charges.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and understanding of helix dipoles.

claim: Backbone nitrogen atoms from αN and αF segments are arranged to coordinate a partially dehydrated Cl− ion near the extracellular end of the constriction (external site or Sext).
source: Backbone nitrogen atoms from αN and αF segments are arranged to coordinate a partially dehydrated Cl− ion near the extracellular end of the constriction (external site or Sext).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: A clear density feature is observed at Sext in the CLC-1 density map, which likely corresponds to a bound Cl− ion.
source: In the CLC-1 density map we observe a clear density feature at Sext, which likely corresponds to a bound Cl− ion (Figure 4A and Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: Scen in CLC proteins has been observed to bind a Cl− ion through polar interactions with one or two backbone nitrogen atoms and the side chains of the conserved tyrosine (TyrC) and serine residues (SerC).
source: Scen has been observed to bind a Cl− ion through polar interactions with one or two backbone nitrogen atoms and the side chains of the conserved tyrosine (denoted TyrC; Y578 of CLC-1 or Y445 of EcCLC) and serine residues (denoted SerC; S189 of CLC-1 or S107 of EcCLC) (Dutzler et al., 2002; Dutzler et al., 2003)
evidence: This is based on cited structural studies.

claim: In the EcCLC transporter, Scen has been shown to bind Cl− relatively strongly (Kd ~1 mM).
source: In the EcCLC transporter, Scen has been shown to bind Cl− relatively strongly (Kd ~1 mM) (Lobet and Dutzler, 2006; Picollo et al., 2009)
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: Sint is largely exposed to the intracellular solvent and binds Cl− with lower affinity (Kd >20 mM).
source: Sint is largely exposed to the intracellular solvent and binds Cl− with lower affinity (Kd >20 mM) (Lobet and Dutzler, 2006; Picollo et al., 2009)
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: In the CLC-1 map (determined in the presence of 116 mM Cl−), Sint shows a density peak whose intensity is comparable to that of the Sext density.
source: In the CLC-1 map (determined in the presence of 116 mM Cl−), Sint shows a density peak whose intensity is comparable to that of the Sext density (Figure 4A and Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: No density for an ion at Scen is observed above the noise level in the CLC-1 map, suggesting that Scen of CLC-1 may have a lower Cl− occupancy than Sext and Sint.
source: By contrast, we do not observe density for an ion at Scen above the noise level, suggesting that Scen of CLC-1 may have a lower Cl− occupancy than Sext and Sint.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map and an inference about occupancy.

claim: The position of TyrC in CLC-1 is shifted away from Scen by ~1.5 Å compared to other CLC proteins.
source: For example, we note that the position of TyrC is shifted away from Scen by ~1.5 Å (see Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Glugate in CLC-1 adopts a notably different conformation than previously observed in CLC transporters.
source: Like transporter-type CLC proteins and in contrast to CLC-K, the CLC-1 channel has a Glugate, but in CLC-1 it adopts a notably different conformation than previously observed in CLC transporters (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Glugate, located in the immediate vicinity of Sext and Scen, plays a key role in ion transport in transporters.
source: Based on previous studies on transporters (Dutzler et al., 2002; Dutzler et al., 2003; Feng et al., 2010), Glugate, located in the immediate vicinity of Sext and Scen, plays a key role in ion transport
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: When deprotonated, Glugate's side-chain carboxylic moiety resides in either the Sext or Scen Cl− binding sites in transporters, preventing the binding of a Cl− ion therein.
source: when deprotonated its side-chain carboxylic moiety resides in either the Sext or Scen Cl− binding sites, preventing the binding of a Cl− ion therein.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional studies of transporters.

claim: In the CLC-1 structure, the Glugate side chain occupies neither Sext nor Scen, but instead it is oriented in a different direction.
source: In the CLC-1 structure, the Glugate side chain occupies neither Sext nor Scen, but instead it is oriented in a different direction.
evidence: This is an observation from the CLC-1 structure.

claim: The difference in Glugate's conformation between CLC-1 and transporters is mainly due to changes in its side-chain rotamer, whereas the polypeptide backbone arrangement in this region is similar among the structures.
source: The difference in Glugate's conformation is mainly due to changes in its side-chain rotamer, whereas the polypeptide backbone arrangement in this region is similar among the structures (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed Glugate conformation in CLC-1 is different than the outwardly-oriented conformation that has been seen in the structure of an EcCLC Glu-to-Gln (E148Q) mutant.
source: The observed Glugate conformation is also different than the outwardly-oriented (side chain projecting into the extracellular funnel) conformation that has been seen in the structure of an EcCLC Glu-to-Gln (E148Q) mutant (Figure 4C), which is hypothesized to mimic the protonated state of Glugate (Dutzler et al., 2003)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with the cited EcCLC mutant structure.

claim: It is unclear whether the Glugate in the CLC-1 structure (determined at pH 7.4) is protonated.
source: It is unclear whether the Glugate in the CLC-1 structure (determined at pH 7.4) is protonated.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the protonation state.

claim: The pKa of the Glugate side chain might be shifted towards a more neutral pH as it is neighbored by multiple hydrophobic amino acids.
source: The pKa of the Glugate side chain might be shifted towards a more neutral pH as it is neighbored by multiple hydrophobic amino acids (Isom et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a speculation based on known effects of hydrophobic environments on pKa, supported by a citation.

claim: Glugate at the observed position in CLC-1 is more likely deprotonated because its side chain seems exposed to water molecules due to the presence of the second intracellular pore.
source: Yet, Glugate at this position is more likely deprotonated because its side chain seems exposed to water molecules due to the presence of the second intracellular pore (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural environment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In CLC transporters, the Glugate conformation observed in CLC-1 would be highly unfavorable because it would produce steric clashes with neighboring side chains.
source: In CLC transporters, this conformation would be highly unfavorable because it would produce steric clashes with neighboring side chains (equivalent to V236, V265, and F279 of CLC-1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which are moved away in CLC-1 by a shift of the αG and αH helices.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conformation of Glugate observed in CLC-1 does not seem possible in CLC transporters studied so far.
source: In other words, this conformation of Glugate does not seem possible in CLC transporters studied so far.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: The observed Glugate conformation of CLC-1 was unexpected because it was never observed in other CLC protein structures.
source: The observed Glugate conformation of CLC-1 was unexpected because it was never observed in other CLC protein structures
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the observation.

claim: The observed Glugate conformation is consistent with an open CLC-1 channel, which is expected in the absence of an applied membrane potential.
source: and yet it is consistent with an open CLC-1 channel, which is expected in the absence of an applied membrane potential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known voltage-gating properties of CLC-1.

claim: CLC-1 is a voltage-gated channel, which closes when the membrane potential is negative.
source: CLC-1 is a voltage-gated channel, which closes when the membrane potential is negative (i.e., at its 'resting' value) (Fahlke et al., 1996; Pusch et al., 1995)
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: In the presence of an applied negative membrane potential, the Glugate side chain in CLC-1 may move into either the Sext or Scen position, as seen in CLC transporters, and prevent Cl− conduction.
source: Perhaps in the presence of an applied negative membrane potential the Glugate side chain moves into either the Sext or Scen position, as seen in CLC transporters, and prevents Cl− conduction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about voltage-dependent gating.

claim: The hypothesis that Glugate moves to block the pore at negative voltages would account for the observation that CLC-1 and related CLC-0 conduct Cl− ions at all membrane voltages when the Glugate residue is mutated to Gln.
source: This possibility would account for the observation that CLC-1 and related CLC-0 conduct Cl− ions at all membrane voltages when the Glugate residue is mutated to Gln (Dutzler et al., 2003; Fahlke et al., 1997)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observation to cited functional data.

claim: The previous CLC-K channel structure has suggested that a wider pore diameter between Scen and Sint is crucial for its channel function.
source: The previous CLC-K channel structure has suggested that a wider pore diameter between Scen and Sint is crucial for its channel function (Park et al., 2017)
evidence: This is based on the cited CLC-K structure study.

claim: In CLC transporters, a kinetic barrier for Cl− passage exists on the intracellular side of the vestibule to preclude slippage of Cl− ions during the Cl−/H+ exchange cycle.
source: In CLC transporters, a kinetic barrier for Cl− passage (i.e., a narrowing of the pore) exists on the intracellular side of the vestibule to preclude slippage of Cl− ions during the Cl−/H+ exchange cycle (Feng et al., 2010)
evidence: This is based on the cited study.

claim: The kinetic barrier in CLC transporters is due to a narrow pore width between Scen and Sint, which is created in part by SerC of the αC-D loop interposed between the two Cl− binding sites.
source: This barrier is due to a narrow pore width between Scen and Sint, which is created in part by SerC of the αC-D loop interposed between the two Cl− binding sites.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of transporters.

claim: In the CLC-K structure, the αC-D loop has a distinctly different conformation, where SerC is flipped down and thus no longer interposed between the two Cl− binding sites.
source: In the CLC-K structure, the αC-D loop has a distinctly different conformation, where SerC is flipped down and thus no longer interposed between the two Cl− binding sites.
evidence: This is based on the CLC-K structure.

claim: In CLC-K, the pore diameter is wider such that Cl− ions will more readily permeate.
source: Consequently, the pore diameter is wider such that Cl− ions will more readily permeate.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation of CLC-K.

claim: In contrast to CLC-K, the αC-D loop in CLC-1 adopts the loop conformation seen in CLC transporters, especially CmCLC.
source: In contrast to CLC-K, the αC-D loop in CLC-1 adopts the loop conformation seen in CLC transporters, especially CmCLC (Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5.

claim: In CLC-1, the SerC side chain is positioned between Sint and Scen.
source: Consequently, the SerC side chain is positioned between Sint and Scen (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the case of CLC-1, the αC-D loop itself does not provide an explanation for why CLC-1 functions as a Cl− channel.
source: Therefore, in the case of CLC-1 the αC-D loop itself does not provide an explanation for why CLC-1 functions as a Cl− channel (see below).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation that the αC-D loop is similar to transporters.

claim: The 'flipped-down' conformation of SerC may be unique to the CLC-K channel.
source: This also suggests that the 'flipped-down' conformation of SerC may be unique to the CLC-K channel.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural comparison.

claim: In both CLC-1 and CLC-K channels, a continuous Cl− pathway was evident in between the extracellular and intracellular funnels, through the selectivity filter.
source: In both CLC-1 and CLC-K channels, a continuous Cl− pathway was evident in between the extracellular and intracellular funnels, through the selectivity filter (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the EcCLC and CmCLC transporters, a continuous pore could be detected only when the Glugate side-chain atoms (from Cβ) were excluded from the pore radius calculation as Glugate sits at Sext or Scen.
source: In the EcCLC and CmCLC transporters, a continuous pore could be detected only when the Glugate side-chain atoms (from Cβ) were excluded from the pore radius calculation as Glugate sits at Sext or Scen (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The CLC-1 channel has the narrowest (1.0 Å in radius) constriction above Sext toward the extracellular side due to the placement of the M485 side chain near the external end of the Cl− pathway.
source: The CLC-1 channel has the narrowest (1.0 Å in radius) constriction above Sext toward the extracellular side due to the placement of the M485 side chain near the external end of the Cl− pathway (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The flexibility of the M485 side chain must allow Cl− ions to pass through the narrow constriction in CLC-1.
source: While the radius is significantly smaller than the Cl− radius (~1.7 Å), the flexibility of the M485 side chain must allow Cl− ions to pass through this region.
evidence: This is an inference about how ions can pass through a narrow constriction.

claim: M485 likely affects the Cl− throughput of the CLC-1 channel.
source: Given the narrowness of this constriction, it is likely that M485 affects the Cl− throughput of the channel.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: Mutation of M485 to valine (M485V) causes recessive myotonia congenita and has been shown to reduce the single channel conductance of CLC-1 to about 20% of the wild type channel conductance.
source: In fact, its mutation to less flexible valine (M485V) causes recessive myotonia congenita and has been shown to reduce the single channel conductance of CLC-1 to about 20% of the wild type channel conductance (Wollnik et al., 1997)
evidence: This is based on the cited functional study.

claim: From Sext to the intracellular opening, the CLC-1 channel structure shows a relatively wide pore opening despite its 'transporter-like' αC-D loop.
source: From Sext to the intracellular opening the CLC-1 channel structure shows a relatively wide pore opening despite its 'transporter-like' αC-D loop.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis.

claim: The relatively wide pore opening in CLC-1 suggests the absence of a large kinetic barrier, but for reasons other than the αC-D loop conformation.
source: This suggests the absence of a large kinetic barrier in CLC-1, but for reasons other than the αC-D loop conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: Compared to the CLC-K channel, CLC-1 has a slightly narrower (1.5 Å vs 1.7 Å in radius) opening between Scen and Sint because of SerC.
source: Compared to the CLC-K channel, CLC-1 has a slightly narrower (1.5 Å vs 1.7 Å in radius) opening between Scen and Sint because of SerC.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis comparing CLC-1 and CLC-K.

claim: The slightly narrower opening in CLC-1 might create a kinetic barrier to some degree, but the pore is still significantly wider and more hydrophilic than the equivalent region in the EcCLC transporter.
source: This might create a kinetic barrier to some degree, but the pore is still significantly wider and more hydrophilic than the equivalent region in the EcCLC transporter (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The difference in pore width between CLC-1 and EcCLC originates mainly from two amino acids (T475 and G483) lining the constriction in CLC-1.
source: The difference originates mainly from two amino acids (T475 and G483) lining the constriction.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: In EcCLC, the positions equivalent to T475 and G483 of CLC-1 are F348 and I356, which project their bulky, hydrophobic side chains towards the Cl− pathway between Scen and Sint.
source: In EcCLC, the equivalent positions are F348 and I356, which project their bulky, hydrophobic side chains towards the Cl− pathway between Scen and Sint.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: In EcCLC, F348 and I356, together with proximal placement of SerC and TyrC, narrow the opening to 1.0 Å in radius.
source: Together with proximal placement of SerC and TyrC, this narrows the opening (1.0 Å in radius) in EcCLC.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis of EcCLC.

claim: In the CmCLC transporter, the constriction at the kinetic barrier region is wider (1.6 Å in radius) than EcCLC because of smaller side chains at the equivalent positions (I421 and V429) and a slight downward shift (1.5 Å) of SerC.
source: In the CmCLC transporter, the constriction at the kinetic barrier region is wider (1.6 Å in radius) than EcCLC because of smaller side chains at the equivalent positions (I421 and V429; Figure 6D) and a slight downward shift (1.5 Å) of SerC with respect to the positions in EcCLC (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis and structural comparison shown in Figures 5B and 6D.

claim: Hydrophobicity provided by the I421 and V429 side chains in CmCLC might result in a significantly higher kinetic barrier than in CLC-1.
source: Yet, hydrophobicity provided by the I421 and V429 side chains might result in a significantly higher kinetic barrier than in CLC-1.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the chemical properties of the residues.

claim: The CLC-1 channel shows a 1.5 Å outward shift of the TyrC side chain with respect to the position that is almost invariant in the other CLC structures.
source: It is noteworthy that the CLC-1 channel shows a 1.5 Å outward shift of the TyrC side chain with respect to the position that is almost invariant in the other CLC structures (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In CLC-1, the shift of TyrC contributes to pore widening in the cytosolic vestibule.
source: In CLC-1, this shift contributes to pore widening in the cytosolic vestibule.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: It is unclear if the shift of TyrC in CLC-1 is static or part of dynamic movements and if it is unique in CLC-1 or a similar movement exists in other CLC proteins.
source: At present it is unclear if this shift of TyrC is static or part of dynamic movements in CLC-1 and if it is unique in CLC-1 or a similar movement exists in other CLC proteins.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the nature of the TyrC shift.

claim: Previous biophysical studies have proposed a movement of TyrC to explain alternating gate opening of the EcCLC Cl−/H+ transporter.
source: Previous biophysical studies have proposed a movement of TyrC to explain alternating gate opening of the EcCLC Cl−/H+ transporter (Basilio et al., 2014; Jayaram et al., 2008; Khantwal et al., 2016)
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: EcCLC crystal structures obtained with a number of different variants and crystallization conditions have not yet revealed any movement of TyrC.
source: On the other hand, EcCLC crystal structures obtained with a number of different variants and crystallization conditions have not yet revealed any movement of TyrC.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural data available for EcCLC.

claim: T475 and G483 of CLC-1 (equivalent to F348 and I356 in EcCLC, respectively) likely contribute to lowering of the kinetic barrier.
source: Because the CLC-1 structure suggests that T475 and G483 (equivalent to F348 and I356 in EcCLC, respectively) likely contribute to lowering of the kinetic barrier, we compared amino acids lining this region among both CLC channels and transporters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: Positions equivalent to T475 and G483 of CLC-1 showed a distinctive differential pattern when comparing CLC channels and transporters.
source: Indeed, these two positions showed a distinctive differential pattern when comparing CLC channels and transporters, whereas other positions (i.e., H369, C481, L577, and I581 in CLC-1) did not.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Generally, the two positions equivalent to T475 and G483 are filled with large, hydrophobic amino acids in transporters but are replaced by a small, polar amino acid in CLC channels.
source: Generally, these two positions are filled with large, hydrophobic amino acids in transporters but are replaced by a small, polar amino acid in CLC channels.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: In CLC-K channels, position 417 (Y425) is an outlier to the pattern, but its phenyl side chain is skewed off the Cl− pathway and does not seem to create a kinetic barrier.
source: One notable outlier is position 417 of the CLC-K channels (Y425). However, the CLC-K channel structure shows that its phenyl side chain is skewed off the Cl− pathway, and thus does not seem to create a kinetic barrier in CLC-K (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of CLC-K shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In CLC-K, Y425 forms the Scen Cl− binding site together with TyrC and F519 through anion-quadrupole interactions.
source: In fact, it forms the Scen Cl− binding site together with TyrC and F519 through anion-quadrupole interactions (Park et al., 2017) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the cited CLC-K structure study and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A lowered barrier in the Scen–Sint region of the pore is a common feature of CLC channels.
source: In summary, the observed amino acid pattern and structural information suggest that a lowered barrier in the Scen–Sint region of the pore is a common feature of CLC channels, but CLC-1 and CLC-K channels achieve this somewhat differently.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and sequence analysis.

claim: In the CLC-1 channel, small side chains in pore-lining residues lower the kinetic barrier.
source: In the CLC-1 channel, small side chains in pore-lining residues lower the kinetic barrier, whereas in CLC-K mainly the reorientation of SerC lowers it.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: In CLC-K, mainly the reorientation of SerC lowers the kinetic barrier.
source: In the CLC-1 channel, small side chains in pore-lining residues lower the kinetic barrier, whereas in CLC-K mainly the reorientation of SerC lowers it.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: The extent of the kinetic barrier should also be affected by the hydrophobic and electrostatic nature of the lining residues, not only the physical dimensions of the pore.
source: The extent of the kinetic barrier should also be affected by the hydrophobic and electrostatic nature of the lining residues, not only the physical dimensions of the pore.
evidence: This is a general principle about factors affecting kinetic barriers.

claim: Channel behavior in CLC proteins arises when Glugate is either absent or allowed to reside in an 'open' configuration for a sufficiently extended period of time.
source: Combining the new structural information and previous data, we propose a working model that channel behavior in CLC proteins arises out of the following physical conditions (Figure 7): (1) Glugate is either absent (i.e., in CLC-K) or allowed to reside in an 'open' configuration (i.e., CLC-1) for a sufficiently extended period of time (rather than occupying Sext or Scen)
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Channel behavior in CLC proteins arises when there is a lowered kinetic barrier between Scen and Sint.
source: Combining the new structural information and previous data, we propose a working model that channel behavior in CLC proteins arises out of the following physical conditions (Figure 7): ... (2) a lowered kinetic barrier between Scen and Sint
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Channel behavior in CLC proteins arises when there is reduced Cl−-binding affinity at Scen or Sext.
source: Combining the new structural information and previous data, we propose a working model that channel behavior in CLC proteins arises out of the following physical conditions (Figure 7): ... (3) reduced Cl−-binding affinity at Scen (or Sext, as suggested by apparent low occupancy in the CLC-K structure).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: A reduced kinetic barrier would be an important feature to achieve fast Cl− throughput in channels.
source: A reduced kinetic barrier would be an important feature to achieve fast Cl− throughput.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional importance of the kinetic barrier.

claim: A sufficient kinetic barrier would be crucial in transporters to preclude undesired slippage of Cl− ions through the transiently open pore.
source: On the other hand, a sufficient kinetic barrier would be crucial in transporters to preclude undesired slippage of Cl− ions through the transiently open pore (Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on the cited mechanistic study.

claim: Reduction of Cl−-binding affinity at Scen and/or Sext might contribute to high Cl− throughput in channels.
source: In addition, reduction of Cl−-binding affinity at Scen and/or Sext, which is energetically related to the kinetic barrier, might also contribute to high Cl− throughput in channels.
evidence: This is a speculation based on energetic considerations.

claim: Relatively deep energy wells at Scen and Sext in EcCLC would create a larger energy difference between the binding sites and the 'transition states', which effectively raises the energy barrier.
source: For example, relatively deep energy wells at Scen and Sext, as implied by the high occupancy of sites in the EcCLC transporter, would create a larger energy difference between the binding sites and the 'transition states', which effectively raises the energy barrier.
evidence: This is an inference based on energetic principles.

claim: In CLC-1, the relatively low binding site occupancy implies not very deep energy wells and thus a smaller energy difference between the binding sites and 'transition states'.
source: In CLC-1 the relatively low binding site occupancy implies not very deep energy wells and thus a smaller energy difference between the binding sites and 'transition states'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed occupancy and energetic principles.

claim: Opening of Glugate alone by the Glu-to-Ala mutation (E148A) in EcCLC abolishes the H+ transport activity.
source: As reported previously (Jayaram et al., 2008), opening of Glugate alone by the Glu-to-Ala mutation (E148A) abolishes the H+ transport activity
evidence: This is based on the cited functional study.

claim: The E148A mutation in EcCLC reduced Cl− throughput by a factor of approximately 0.25.
source: but it also reduced Cl− throughput by a factor of approximately 0.25.
evidence: This is based on functional data from the cited study.

claim: The E148A mutant of EcCLC still retains the kinetic barrier deterring Cl− ions from moving between Scen and Sint.
source: We reason that this is likely because the mutant still retains the kinetic barrier deterring Cl− ions from moving between Scen and Sint.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the functional data.

claim: Removal of the Glugate is sufficient to convert the transporter into a Cl− channel.
source: Thus, while removal of the Glugate is sufficient to convert the transporter into a Cl− channel, a reduced kinetic barrier would be key to an increased Cl− throughput, an important feature of the native CLC channels.
evidence: This is based on functional data.

claim: A reduced kinetic barrier would be key to an increased Cl− throughput, an important feature of the native CLC channels.
source: Thus, while removal of the Glugate is sufficient to convert the transporter into a Cl− channel, a reduced kinetic barrier would be key to an increased Cl− throughput, an important feature of the native CLC channels.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional experiments.

claim: Trimming the side chain of SerC (S107G) in EcCLC increased the Cl− transport rate by a factor of 2.
source: Trimming the side chain of SerC (S107G), with the intention of mimicking the flipped SerC in the CLC-K channel, increased the Cl− transport rate by a factor of 2, as previously reported (Jayaram et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8 and cited reference.

claim: The S107G mutation in EcCLC lowered H+ coupling 3-fold.
source: At the same time, this mutation lowered H+ coupling 3-fold, as one would expect due to the slippage of uncoupled Cl− ions.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The S107G/F348A double mutant of EcCLC increased the Cl− throughput and almost abolished coupled H+ transport.
source: Next, since CLC-K has a polar amino acid (Thr) at one of its pore-lining residues (F348 of EcCLC), we further introduced a similar (F348A) mutation. This increased the Cl− throughput and almost abolished coupled H+ transport.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The S107G/F348A/E148A triple mutant of EcCLC has a Cl− transport rate increased about 25-fold compared to the E148A single mutant.
source: Finally, by adding a Glugate mutation (E148A) to this double mutant the Cl− throughput was further increased. Compared to the E148A single mutant, the triple mutant (S107G/F348A/E148A) has a Cl− transport rate increased about 25-fold (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single mutations at the pore-lining amino acids (F348T or I356G) in EcCLC did not increase the Cl− transport rate.
source: While single mutations at the pore-lining amino acids (F348T or I356G) did not increase the Cl− transport rate, the double mutation (F348T/I356G) moderately increased the Cl− throughput (1.5-fold with respect to the wildtype).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The F348T/I356G double mutant of EcCLC moderately increased the Cl− throughput (1.5-fold with respect to the wildtype).
source: While single mutations at the pore-lining amino acids (F348T or I356G) did not increase the Cl− transport rate, the double mutation (F348T/I356G) moderately increased the Cl− throughput (1.5-fold with respect to the wildtype).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The F348T/I356G double mutant of EcCLC displayed no measurable H+ transport activity.
source: We note that this mutant displayed no measurable H+ transport activity.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The F348T/I356G/E148A triple mutant of EcCLC dramatically increased Cl− throughput (22-fold with respect to the single E148A mutant).
source: When the double mutant was combined with the Glugate mutation (E148A), which was used as a surrogate of the Glugate conformation observed in the CLC-1 structure, the Cl− throughput dramatically increased (22-fold with respect to the single E148A mutant; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single mutations (F348T or I356G) in the E148A background of EcCLC showed intermediate increases in Cl− throughput, suggesting that the effects of these mutations are somewhat additive.
source: Single mutations (F348T or I356G) in the E148A background showed intermediate increases in Cl− throughput, suggesting that the effects of these mutations are somewhat additive.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The human CLC-1 channel exhibits interesting structural differences in the Cl− transport pathway and the gates, which can explain why this protein functions as a Cl− channel instead of a Cl−/H+ antiporter.
source: The human CLC-1 channel exhibits interesting structural differences in the Cl− transport pathway and the gates, which can explain why this protein functions as a Cl− channel instead of a Cl−/H+ antiporter.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The outer gate of the CLC-1 channel remains open because the carboxylic side-chain Glugate is located off to the side, away from the Cl− transport pathway.
source: The outer gate of the channel remains open because the carboxylic side-chain Glugate is located off to the side, away from the Cl− transport pathway (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the structural observation shown in Figure 4.

claim: The inner kinetic barrier in CLC-1 seems to be substantially lowered compared to transporters owing to a wider pore diameter near the cytosolic side.
source: The inner kinetic barrier seems to be substantially lowered compared to transporters owing to a wider pore diameter near the cytosolic side (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The pore widening in CLC-1 is subtle, but distinctive enough to reveal a pattern separating channels and transporters at the protein sequence level.
source: The pore widening is subtle, but distinctive enough to reveal a pattern separating channels and transporters at the protein sequence level (independent of the presence or absence of a Glugate) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The position of the Glugate residue in CLC-1 is unique among CLC structures so far observed.
source: The position of the Glugate residue in CLC-1 is unique among CLC structures so far observed.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The new Glugate position in CLC-1 is enabled by a pocket that is large and hydrophilic enough to accommodate Glugate's side chain.
source: The new Glugate position, where its carboxylic side chain is directed off to the side of the Cl− pathway, is enabled by a pocket that is large and hydrophilic (owing to its bifurcated pore structure) enough to accommodate Glugate's side chain.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The pocket that accommodates Glugate's side chain in CLC-1 may also exist in other Glugate-containing CLC channels (i.e., CLC-0 and CLC-2) but does not seem to exist in transporters because of a different arrangement of neighboring amino acids.
source: This pocket may also exist in other Glugate-containing CLC channels (i.e., CLC-0 and CLC-2) but does not seem to exist in transporters because of a different arrangement of neighboring amino acids.
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence and structural comparison.

claim: The Glugate position observed in CLC-1 is likely key to understanding why CLC-1 exhibits a stable open (i.e., conducting) state.
source: It seems likely that this Glugate position is key to understanding why CLC-1 exhibits a stable open (i.e., conducting) state.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: The Glugate in CLC-0 and CLC-1 has been identified as a 'voltage sensor' because its removal abolishes voltage-dependent gating.
source: On the basis of mutagenesis studies (Dutzler et al., 2003; Fahlke et al., 1997), the Glugate in CLC-0 and CLC-1 has been identified as a 'voltage sensor' because its removal abolishes voltage-dependent gating.
evidence: This is based on cited mutagenesis studies.

claim: The position of Glugate (i.e., whether it resides off to the side, not occluding the pore, or within the pore) depends on the transmembrane voltage and generally dictates gating each CLC-1 monomer's pore.
source: From this observation, we would suggest that the position of Glugate (i.e., whether it resides off to the side, not occluding the pore, or within the pore) depends on the transmembrane voltage and generally dictates gating each CLC-1 monomer's pore (also referred to as a 'protopore').
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observation and functional data.

claim: If the Glugate conformation in CLC-1 corresponds to the conducting state, it is unclear how it is favored by low pH outside.
source: An unresolved issue raised by the new Glugate side chain conformation is this: if this conformation corresponds to the conducting state, how is it favored by low pH outside (Rychkov et al., 1996)?
evidence: This is a question raised by the structural observation in light of cited functional data.

claim: One possibility is the Glugate might be protonated in the conformation observed in CLC-1.
source: One possibility is the Glugate might be protonated in this conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Low pH might stabilize a conformation of Glugate outside the pore, as in the EcCLC E148Q mutant.
source: Alternatively, low pH might stabilize a conformation of Glugate outside the pore, as in the EcCLC E148Q mutant.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The pH effect on CLC-1 might be produced allosterically by protonation of an unidentified amino acid on the extracellular side.
source: Finally, the pH effect might be produced allosterically by protonation of an unidentified amino acid on the extracellular side.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Both CLC-2 and CLC-K channels are inhibited by external pH <6.5, and a His residue (H532 of CLC-2 and H497 of CLC-K), located ~20 Å away from the pore, is responsible for this effect.
source: For example, both CLC-2 and CLC-K channels are inhibited by external pH <6.5, but it has been shown that a His residue (H532 of CLC-2 and H497 of CLC-K), which is located ~20 Å away from the pore, is responsible for this effect (Gradogna et al., 2010; Niemeyer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: Functional experiments using EcCLC provide support for the model that a low kinetic barrier in the cytosolic vestibule is necessary for high Cl− transport rates.
source: Functional experiments using EcCLC provide support for our model that a low kinetic barrier in the cytosolic vestibule is necessary for high Cl− transport rates, which are general characteristics of native CLC channels (Figure 8 and also see (Jayaram et al., 2008)).
evidence: This is based on the functional data shown in Figure 8 and cited reference.

claim: A small increase in the pore diameter and a decrease in hydrophobicity of the pore lining can substantially lower the kinetic barrier.
source: The results indicate that a small increase in the pore diameter and a decrease in hydrophobicity of the pore lining can substantially lower the kinetic barrier.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the functional experiments.

claim: The extent of the kinetic barrier might be somewhat less in the CLC-1 channel than in the CLC-K channel because of CLC-1's SerC 'transporter-like' conformation.
source: The structures, however, suggest that the extent might be somewhat less in the CLC-1 channel than in the CLC-K channel because of CLC-1's SerC 'transporter-like' conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural comparison.

claim: CLC-1 has vestigial H+ transport activity.
source: This is in fact consistent with the observation that CLC-1 has vestigial H+ transport activity (Picollo and Pusch, 2005)
evidence: This is based on the cited functional study.

claim: CLC-1 has a relatively slow Cl− throughput compared to that of CLC-K channels (1.2–1.8 pS versus 20–30 pS of CLC-K).
source: and a relatively slow Cl− throughput compared to that of CLC-K channels (1.2–1.8 pS versus 20–30 pS of CLC-K) (L'Hoste et al., 2013; Saviane et al., 1999; Scholl et al., 2006; Weinreich and Jentsch, 2001)
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: In CLC-K, position 425 contains a bulky amino acid (Y425), in contrast to other CLC proteins.
source: In CLC-K, position 425 contains a bulky amino acid (Y425), in contrast to other CLC proteins.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural comparison.

claim: In the canonical conformation, SerC would sterically clash with Y425 in CLC-K.
source: In the canonical conformation SerC would sterically clash with Y425 (e.g., the center-to-center distance between the SerC-Oγ and Y425-Cε atoms would become 2.3 Å).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The steric incompatibility imposed by the unique Y425 might lead to the flipped-down conformation of SerC in the CLC-K channel.
source: We speculate that this steric incompatibility imposed by the unique Y425 might lead to the flipped-down conformation of SerC in the CLC-K channel.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: The observed low Cl− occupancy at Scen in the CLC-1 structure has a striking resemblance to previous crystallographic observations on EcCLC, wherein Scen remained unoccupied when experiments were performed with TyrC mutants lacking H+ transport activity or with pseudohalides.
source: The observed low Cl− occupancy at Scen in the CLC-1 structure has a striking resemblance to previous crystallographic observations on EcCLC, wherein Scen remained unoccupied when experiments were performed with TyrC mutants lacking H+ transport activity or with pseudohalides, which permeate without coupled H+ transport (Accardi et al., 2006; Nguitragool and Miller, 2006)
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited structural studies.

claim: In EcCLC, low Cl− occupancy correlates with low anion binding affinity.
source: It has been shown that in EcCLC, low Cl− occupancy correlates with low anion binding affinity (Picollo et al., 2009)
evidence: This is based on the cited functional study.

claim: The comparison with EcCLC suggests a reduced Cl− binding affinity at Scen in CLC-1.
source: This comparison suggests a reduced Cl− binding affinity at Scen in CLC-1, although further biophysical measurements will be necessary to confirm this.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation and comparison with EcCLC data.

claim: Reduced Cl− binding affinity at Scen in CLC-1 contributes to reduced H+ transport and increased Cl− conduction.
source: We speculate that this feature contributes to reduced H+ transport and increased Cl− conduction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Possible causes underlying the altered Cl− affinity in CLC-1 include the shifted position of TyrC and subtle changes in positions and orientations of neighboring backbone nitrogen atoms coordinating the Cl− ion.
source: Possible causes underlying the altered Cl− affinity include the shifted position of TyrC and subtle changes in positions and orientations of neighboring backbone nitrogen atoms coordinating the Cl− ion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: CLC-0/1/2 channels have smaller, more flexible residues (Gly or Ala) at the G483 position, in contrast to Leu, Ile, or Val in CLC transporters.
source: For example, we note that CLC-0/1/2 channels have smaller, more flexible residues (Gly or Ala) at the G483 position, in contrast to Leu, Ile, or Val in CLC transporters.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: CLC-1 is now the second structure of a channel-forming CLC, the first being CLC-K.
source: CLC-1 is now the second structure of a channel-forming CLC, the first being CLC-K (Park et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the structural knowledge.

claim: One of the major features giving rise to channel behavior in CLC proteins is a more conductive pore.
source: One of the major features giving rise to channel behavior is a more conductive pore.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural comparison.

claim: The structural differences giving rise to the higher Cl− conductivity in CLC channels are fairly subtle: the pore is slightly wider and the chemical properties a little different, accounting for a reduced kinetic barrier.
source: The structural differences giving rise to the higher Cl− conductivity are fairly subtle: the pore is slightly wider and the chemical properties a little different, accounting for what we propose to be a reduced kinetic barrier.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Throughput rates in the range of 106 ions per second do not require a wide pore.
source: Throughput rates in the range of 106 ions per second do not require a wide pore.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the structural observations.

claim: As long as the pore lining atoms are favorable to a conducting ion with respect to their electrostatic and chemical properties, and as long as they are sufficiently dynamic, then the ion can diffuse through even if the pore in places is on average narrower than the ion.
source: We conclude that even if the pore in places is on average narrower than the ion, as long as the lining atoms are favorable to a conducting ion with respect to their electrostatic and chemical properties, and as long as they are sufficiently dynamic (i.e. they can move out of the way), then the ion can diffuse through.
evidence: This is a general principle concluded from the structural analysis.

claim: The atomic structures of K+ channels show that the pore's radius between the K+ binding sites is smaller than the radius of a K+ ion, yet some K+ channels approach throughput rates of 108 per second.
source: We offer as an example of this idea, the selectivity filter of K+ channels (Zhou et al., 2001). The atomic structures show us that in fact the pore's radius between the K+ binding sites is smaller than the radius of a K+ ion. And yet some K+ channels approach throughput rates of 108 per second.
evidence: This is based on the cited structural study of K+ channels.

claim: The radius of the pore in CLC channels and transporters is not very different.
source: It is not surprising to now understand that the radius of the pore in CLC channels and transporters is not very different.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural comparison.

claim: The structures of CLC-1 and CLC-K channels support the idea that CLC channels are 'broken transporters'.
source: The structures of CLC-1 and CLC-K channels support the idea that CLC channels are 'broken transporters' (Jayaram et al., 2008; Lísal and Maduke, 2008; Miller, 2006), where their channel function is built upon a transporter structure with modifications of the gates.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the structural data and cited references.

claim: The structures demonstrate that relatively small changes in the active site and ion transport pathway of a transporter gives rise to channel function.
source: The structures demonstrate that relatively small changes in the active site and ion transport pathway of a transporter gives rise to channel function.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural comparison.
